prompt: In ligand field theory, why is the metal's valence s orbital a good candidate for sigma bonding with ligands in any coordination geometry?

choices.text: It is non-directional, so a sigma-donating ligand overlaps with it equally well wherever the ligand is located
It points directly along the x, y and z axes
choices.why: That describes the three p orbitals. The s orbital is spherical and has no preferred direction.

choices.text: It is lower in energy than the ligand donor orbitals
choices.why: The ligand donor orbitals lie lower than the metal orbitals because the donor atoms are more electronegative. The s orbital's advantage is its shape.

choices.text: It can form pi bonds as well as sigma bonds
choices.why: A spherical s orbital can't form pi bonds. Its value is that its sigma overlap doesn't depend on where the ligand sits.

explanation: The s orbital is non-directional: no matter where a sigma-donating ligand is located, it has the same overlap with the spherical s orbital. That makes s a good sigma-bonding partner in any geometry. In an octahedron, the three p orbitals also point along the metal–ligand axes.

prompt: In a sigma-only ligand field picture of an octahedral complex, with ligands on the x, y and z axes, which metal orbitals are left nonbonding?

choices.text: d_xy, d_xz and d_yz
d_z^2 and d_x^2−y^2
choices.why: These two d orbitals lie along the axes and overlap with the ligand donor orbitals, forming sigma bonding and antibonding combinations.

choices.text: The three p orbitals
choices.why: All three p orbitals lie along the axes where the ligands are, so they overlap well with the ligand orbitals.

choices.text: The s orbital
choices.why: The non-directional s orbital overlaps with sigma donors in any geometry.

explanation: The s, the three p, and the d_z^2 and d_x^2−y^2 orbitals overlap with the six ligand donor orbitals. The d_xy, d_xz and d_yz orbitals lie between the axes, have no sigma overlap with the ligands, and remain nonbonding. They become the lower set of d levels, with the sigma-antibonding d_z^2 and d_x^2−y^2 above them.

prompt: When a ligand donor orbital combines with a metal orbital, the donor orbital starts lower in energy. Which statement about the resulting molecular orbitals is correct?

choices.text: The bonding orbital is mostly ligand in character, and the antibonding orbital is mostly metal in character
The bonding orbital is mostly metal in character, and the antibonding orbital is mostly ligand in character
choices.why: Each molecular orbital most resembles the atomic orbital closest to it in energy. The lower-lying ligand orbital dominates the bonding combination.

choices.text: Both orbitals are an equal mix of metal and ligand
choices.why: Equal mixing happens when the two atomic orbitals have the same energy. Here the more electronegative donor atom's orbital is lower, so the mixing is unequal.

choices.text: The bonding orbital is entirely metal, and the antibonding orbital is entirely ligand
choices.why: Both orbitals are mixtures. The bonding one has more ligand character, the antibonding one more metal character.

explanation: The donor atom is more electronegative than the transition metal, so its orbital is lower in energy. In the in-phase (bonding) combination it gets the larger coefficient; in the out-of-phase (antibonding) combination the metal does. So the σ orbital is treated as ligand-centered and σ* as metal-centered.

prompt: How does the strength of a ligand's sigma donation affect the gap between the nonbonding and antibonding d orbitals in an octahedral complex?

choices.text: Stronger sigma donors give a larger gap, because the lower the bonding orbitals sink, the higher the antibonding orbitals rise
Stronger sigma donors give a smaller gap, because they fill the antibonding orbitals
choices.why: The donated electrons go into the bonding orbitals. Stronger bonding pushes the antibonding level up, widening the gap.

choices.text: Sigma donor strength has no effect; only pi interactions change the gap
choices.why: Sigma donor strength matters: strong sigma donors give a large d–d gap and weak ones a small gap.

choices.text: Stronger sigma donors lower the nonbonding d orbitals
choices.why: The nonbonding d orbitals don't interact with sigma donors. It's the antibonding level that rises.

explanation: The stability of the bonding orbitals is reflected in the antibonding level: the lower the bonding electrons sink, the higher the antibonding levels rise. So strong sigma donors give a large gap between the nonbonding and antibonding d orbitals, and weak sigma donors a small one. More basic ligands are often stronger donors.

prompt: A ligand with a second lone pair can pi donate into the metal's d_xy, d_xz and d_yz orbitals. What happens to the d orbital splitting?

choices.text: It becomes smaller, because the d_xy, d_xz and d_yz orbitals become pi antibonding and are pushed up in energy
It becomes larger, because the d_xy, d_xz and d_yz orbitals are lowered in energy
choices.why: Lowering of those orbitals happens with pi acceptors such as CO. With a pi donor, the ligand lone pairs are lower in energy, so the metal-based combinations are pushed up.

choices.text: It is unchanged, because pi bonding uses the metal p orbitals
choices.why: The metal p orbitals are already busy with sigma bonding. The pi interaction uses the d_xy, d_xz and d_yz, which changes the splitting.

choices.text: It becomes smaller, because the d_z^2 and d_x^2−y^2 orbitals are lowered
choices.why: Pi donation involves the d_xy, d_xz and d_yz orbitals; it raises them toward the sigma-antibonding pair.

explanation: The ligand lone pairs lie below the metal d orbitals. The bonding combinations have more ligand character, and the antibonding combinations, still mostly d_xy, d_xz and d_yz, rise in energy. This narrows the gap to the d_z^2 and d_x^2−y^2 orbitals, so a pi donor gives a smaller splitting than a simple sigma donor.

prompt: A metal with d electrons forms a pi bond to carbon monoxide by donating into the empty CO π* orbital. What are the effects of this interaction?

choices.text: The metal d_xy, d_xz and d_yz orbitals drop in energy, increasing the d orbital splitting, and the C–O bond gets weaker
The metal d_xy, d_xz and d_yz orbitals rise in energy, decreasing the splitting, and the C–O bond gets weaker
choices.why: A rise in those orbitals happens with pi donors. The CO π* orbital lies above the metal d orbitals, so the metal-based pi combination is lowered.

choices.text: The d orbitals drop in energy, increasing the splitting, and the C–O bond gets stronger
choices.why: Populating the CO π* orbital breaks part of the C–O pi bond, weakening it.

choices.text: Nothing changes, because no electrons occupy the ligand π* orbital beforehand
choices.why: The empty π* orbital is what accepts the metal's electrons. That lowers the metal's d electrons and changes the splitting.

explanation: A pi acceptor needs an empty orbital of pi symmetry, a π* orbital, which requires a π bond within the ligand; CO is the classic example. The π* orbital lies above the metal d orbitals, so the metal–ligand pi bonding combination has more metal character and lies lower: the d electrons drop into an energy well and the splitting increases. Electrons donated into CO π* weaken the C–O bond.

prompt: As a rough trend, how does the d orbital splitting depend on the type of ligand?

choices.text: pi donors < sigma donors < pi acceptors
pi acceptors < sigma donors < pi donors
choices.why: This is reversed. Pi acceptors lower the d_xy, d_xz and d_yz orbitals and widen the gap; pi donors raise them and narrow it.

choices.text: sigma donors < pi donors < pi acceptors
choices.why: Pi donation narrows the gap compared with simple sigma donation, so pi donors come first.

choices.text: All three types give about the same splitting
choices.why: The three types give clearly different splittings: in Cr(III) complexes, Δo grows from 13,600 cm^−1 for chloride to 26,300 cm^−1 for cyanide.

explanation: Pi donation into the d_xy, d_xz and d_yz orbitals raises them and shrinks the splitting; pi acceptance lowers them and enlarges it. The order is pi donors < sigma donors < pi acceptors, as a rough trend; individual ligands may deviate for other reasons, such as the strength of their sigma donation.

prompt: For sigma bonding in an octahedral complex, the ligand orbitals give Γ = A1g + T1u + Eg. Which metal orbitals match the T1u representation?

choices.text: The three p orbitals
The s orbital
choices.why: The s orbital matches A1g, the totally symmetric representation (x^2 + y^2 + z^2).

choices.text: d_z^2 and d_x^2−y^2
choices.why: These two d orbitals match Eg.

choices.text: d_xy, d_xz and d_yz
choices.why: These have T2g symmetry, which doesn't appear in Γ. That's why they are nonbonding in the sigma-only picture.

explanation: In the O_h character table, (x, y, z) belong to T1u, so the three p orbitals match T1u. A1g corresponds to the s orbital, Eg to d_z^2 and d_x^2−y^2, and the T2g set (d_xy, d_xz, d_yz) has no ligand partner. Group theory reproduces the result found by deciding which orbitals overlap.

prompt: For pi bonding in an octahedral complex (h = 48), the reducible representation has character 12 under E, −4 under the 3C2 (= C4^2) class, and 0 under every other class. T2g has characters 3 under E and −1 under 3C2 (= C4^2). Using a_i = (1/h) Σ N∙χ(R)∙χ_i(R), how many times does T2g appear in this representation?
explanation: Only E and 3C2 (= C4^2) have nonzero characters in Γπ: a(T2g) = (1/48)[1∙12∙3 + 3∙(−4)∙(−1)] = (1/48)(36 + 12) = 48/48 = 1. So the d_xy, d_xz and d_yz set (T2g) has the right symmetry for pi bonding with the ligands.

prompt: In an octahedral complex, d^1 to d^3 ions simply fill the t2g level. For a d^4 ion, what distinguishes the low-spin configuration from the high-spin one?

choices.text: In low spin, the fourth electron pairs in a t2g orbital; in high spin, it goes unpaired into an eg orbital
In low spin, the fourth electron goes into an eg orbital; in high spin, it pairs in a t2g orbital
choices.why: This is reversed. Pairing in t2g lowers the net spin, so that's the low-spin case.

choices.text: Low spin has four unpaired electrons and high spin has two
choices.why: Low-spin d^4 (t2g^4) has two unpaired electrons; high-spin d^4 (t2g^3 eg^1) has four.

choices.text: Low spin means the electrons have smaller individual spins
choices.why: Every electron has the same spin magnitude. High and low spin refer to the net spin, which drops when electrons pair.

explanation: The fourth electron can pair in the lower t2g level (low spin), at the cost of repulsion with the other electron in that orbital, or occupy an eg orbital (high spin), at higher orbital energy but without pairing. The terms refer to the net spin: paired electrons cancel and lower it.

prompt: With strong donors, octahedral Cr^2+ (d^4) adopts a low-spin configuration with all four electrons in the t2g level. Using μ_so = √(n(n + 2)), what is its spin-only magnetic moment, in BM?
explanation: t2g^4 puts one electron in each of the three t2g orbitals and pairs the fourth, leaving n = 2 unpaired electrons. μ_so = √(2 × 4) = √8 = 2.83 BM. With weak donors, high-spin Cr^2+ would have four unpaired electrons instead.

prompt: Δo is 7,500 cm^−1 for [Mn(OH2)6]^2+ and 21,000 cm^−1 for [Mn(OH2)6]^3+; the Cr and Fe aqua ions show the same pattern. What trend does this illustrate?

choices.text: The higher the charge on the metal ion, the larger Δo becomes
The higher the charge on the metal ion, the smaller Δo becomes
choices.why: In each pair, the M(III) ion has the larger splitting.

choices.text: Δo depends only on the ligand, not the metal ion
choices.why: Same ligand, same metal, different charge, and Δo nearly triples for Mn. The metal ion's charge matters.

choices.text: Δo increases steadily from left to right across the first row
choices.why: The section says comparisons between metals in different columns are complicated, with no simple trend. The clear trend here is with charge.

explanation: For Cr, Mn and Fe aqua ions, the M(III) complex always has a significantly larger Δo than the M(II) complex: the higher the charge, the larger Δo. Comparisons between different metals are complicated and show no simple trend.

prompt: Why are complexes of second- and third-row transition metals usually low spin?

choices.text: Δo is much larger for second-row metals than first-row metals, and larger still for third-row metals, so it usually exceeds the pairing energy
Their pairing energies are much larger than those of first-row metals
choices.why: A larger pairing energy would favor high spin. The heavier metals are low spin because their Δo is large compared with the pairing energy.

choices.text: They have no electrons in the eg level
choices.why: Spin state depends on how Δo compares with the pairing energy. A large Δo is what keeps electrons out of eg.

choices.text: They always bind pi-acceptor ligands
choices.why: The comparison is made with identical ligands: Δo for [Rh(NH3)6]^3+ (33,900 cm^−1) is well above [Co(NH3)6]^3+ (23,000 cm^−1). The period itself matters.

explanation: With identical ligands, Δo increases down a group: [Co(NH3)6]^3+ 23,000 cm^−1 < [Rh(NH3)6]^3+ 33,900 cm^−1, and [RhCl6]^3− 20,300 cm^−1 < [IrCl6]^3− 24,900 cm^−1. Pairing energies are not large compared with these values, so second- and third-row ions are usually low spin. First-row ions, with smaller Δo, are often high spin.

prompt: Four octahedral Cr(III) complexes are [CrCl6]^3−, [Cr(OH2)6]^3+, [Cr(NH3)6]^3+ and [Cr(CN)6]^3−. Which order of Δo, from smallest to largest, matches the ligand classes in this section?

choices.why: This is reversed. Cyanide is a pi acceptor and gives the largest splitting; chloride is a pi donor and gives the smallest.
Ammine is a simple sigma donor, while aquo and chloro ligands are pi donors, so ammine gives a larger splitting than either.
Water is a pi donor and ammine a simple sigma donor, so the ammine complex has the larger Δo.

explanation: Pi donors give the smallest splittings and pi acceptors the largest. The measured values follow that: [CrCl6]^3− 13,600 cm^−1 (pi donor), [Cr(OH2)6]^3+ about 17,400 cm^−1 (pi donor), [Cr(NH3)6]^3+ 21,600 cm^−1 (sigma donor), [Cr(CN)6]^3− 26,300 cm^−1 (pi acceptor).

prompt: Chloride and bromide are both pi donors, yet chloride gives a larger field splitting than bromide when coordinated to Ni(II). Why?

choices.text: Chloride is more basic, so it coordinates more strongly, lowering the donor electrons and raising the σ* orbital further
Bromide is a pi acceptor
choices.why: Bromide, like chloride, donates lone pairs; it has no empty π* orbital to accept electrons.

choices.text: Chloride is less basic than bromide
choices.why: The conjugate acids show the reverse: pKa about −6 for HCl versus −9 for HBr, so chloride is the more basic of the two.

choices.text: Chloride is a chelating ligand
choices.why: Chloride binds through a single atom. The difference comes from basicity within the same ligand class.

explanation: Among ligands of the same class, basicity often predicts donor strength. HCl (pKa −6) is a weaker acid than HBr (pKa −9), so chloride is more basic. Stronger coordination puts the donor electrons lower and pushes the σ* orbital higher than with bromide, giving a larger splitting.

prompt: The total pairing energy Π has a coulombic part, Πc, and an exchange part, Πe. What are the signs of these two contributions?

choices.text: Πc is positive, from repulsion between two electrons in the same orbital; Πe is negative, because exchange between like spins lowers the energy
Πc is negative and Πe is positive
choices.why: This is reversed. Repulsion raises the energy (Πc positive), and exchange between like spins lowers it (Πe negative).

choices.text: Both are positive, since pairing always costs energy
choices.why: Exchange is a stabilizing factor: when two electrons of like spin can exchange, the energy decreases.

choices.text: Both are negative, since electrons in the same orbital attract
choices.why: Electrons repel each other. Two electrons in the same orbital raise the energy, making Πc positive.

explanation: Πc arises from repulsion between two electrons occupying the same region of space, so it raises the energy. Πe comes from quantum mechanical exchange between electrons of like spin; it lowers the energy, so it is a negative quantity.

prompt: In an octahedral d^3 ion, the three t2g electrons occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins. Counting each pair of like-spin electrons that can exchange with each other, how many exchanges are possible?
explanation: Label the electrons 1, 2 and 3. The possible pairs are 1–2, 1–3 and 2–3: three exchanges. A d^2 ion has just one, so adding the third electron triples the exchange and significantly lowers the energy.

prompt: For [Fe(OH2)6]^2+ (d^6), Δo = 10,000 cm^−1 and the pairing energy Π = 17,600 cm^−1. Low-spin d^6 (t2g^6) has LFSE −2.4Δo and three electron pairs; high-spin d^6 (t2g^4 eg^2) has LFSE −0.4Δo and one pair. Treating Π as the cost of each pair, what is E(low spin) − E(high spin), in cm^−1?
explanation: ΔE = (−2.4Δo + 3Π) − (−0.4Δo + Π) = −2.0Δo + 2Π = −2.0(10,000) + 2(17,600) = −20,000 + 35,200 = +15,200 cm^−1. The low-spin configuration is higher in energy, so the complex is high spin: pairing costs more than promoting electrons to eg.

prompt: For [Fe(OH2)6]^3+ (d^5), Δo = 14,000 cm^−1 and the pairing energy Π = 30,000 cm^−1. Predict its spin state. How many unpaired electrons does it have?
explanation: Π (30,000 cm^−1) is much larger than Δo (14,000 cm^−1), so it costs more to pair electrons than to promote them to eg. The complex is high spin, t2g^3 eg^2, with all 5 d electrons unpaired.

prompt: Why are many first-row transition metal ions high spin?

choices.text: Their pairing energies are larger than most of their Δo values, so pairing costs more than placing an electron in eg
Their Δo values are larger than their pairing energies
choices.why: That situation would favor low spin. First-row ions are often high spin because Δo is the smaller of the two.

choices.text: They have too few d electrons to pair
choices.why: First-row ions can have up to ten d electrons; the question is whether pairing in t2g costs more than promotion to eg.

choices.text: Their ligands are always pi acceptors
choices.why: Pi acceptors enlarge Δo and favor low spin. The section explains first-row high spin by comparing pairing energy with Δo.

explanation: Total pairing energies for first-row ions (for example 25,500 cm^−1 for [Mn(OH2)6]^2+ and 17,600 cm^−1 for [Fe(OH2)6]^2+) are larger than most first-row Δo values (7,500 and 10,000 cm^−1 for those ions). Pairing then costs more than promotion to eg, so the ions are high spin.

prompt: Each t2g electron contributes −0.4Δo and each eg electron +0.6Δo to the ligand field stabilization energy. What is the LFSE of a low-spin octahedral d^6 ion, in units of Δo?
explanation: Low-spin d^6 is t2g^6 eg^0: LFSE = [0.6(0) − 0.4(6)]Δo = −2.4Δo. The high-spin configuration (t2g^4 eg^2) has only −0.4Δo.

prompt: [Ni(NH3)6]^2+ is an octahedral d^8 complex with Δo = 10,800 cm^−1. Each t2g electron contributes −0.4Δo and each eg electron +0.6Δo. What is its LFSE, in cm^−1?
explanation: d^8 is t2g^6 eg^2 (high and low spin are the same for d^8). LFSE = [0.6(2) − 0.4(6)]Δo = (1.2 − 2.4)Δo = −1.2Δo = −1.2 × 10,800 cm^−1 = −12,960 cm^−1.

prompt: Heats of hydration of the M^2+ ions become more negative across the first transition series, but Ca^2+, Mn^2+ and Zn^2+ lie above the trend (less negative). Why these three?

choices.text: They are d^0, high-spin d^5 and d^10, the configurations with zero ligand field stabilization energy
They are the largest ions in the series
choices.why: The general Coulomb's-law trend comes from ions shrinking across the row. These three stand out because they lack LFSE.

choices.text: They have the most unpaired electrons
choices.why: Ca^2+ and Zn^2+ have no unpaired electrons. What the three share is an LFSE of zero.

choices.text: They form low-spin aqua complexes
choices.why: The analysis assumes high-spin configurations, common for the first row. In high spin, d^0, d^5 and d^10 all have zero LFSE.

explanation: The overall trend follows Coulomb's law: ions get smaller across the row and release more energy on binding water. Ions with LFSE get extra stabilization in an octahedral environment and sit below the trend. Ca^2+ (d^0), Mn^2+ (high-spin d^5, t2g^3 eg^2) and Zn^2+ (d^10) have zero LFSE, so they lie above it.

prompt: Hydration energies don't track LFSE perfectly. One reason is the nephelauxetic ("cloud-expanding") effect. What is it?

choices.text: Interelectron repulsion in a complex can be lower than in the free ion, depending on the degree of covalency
Pairing energy increases when an ion's charge increases
choices.why: That trend (often, but not always) reflects contraction of more highly charged ions. The nephelauxetic effect concerns reduced repulsion in complexes.

choices.text: The d orbital splitting becomes larger with pi-acceptor ligands
choices.why: That is the effect of pi acceptors on Δo, not the nephelauxetic effect.

choices.text: The ions get smaller across a row of the periodic table
choices.why: Shrinking ions explain the general Coulomb's-law trend in hydration energies, not the nephelauxetic effect.

explanation: The name means "cloud-expanding": in a complex, interelectron repulsion can be lower than in the free ion, depending on the degree of covalency. It is one of several factors besides LFSE that affect observed hydration energies.

prompt: In a tetrahedral complex, with the ligands at alternating corners of a cube, how are the d orbitals split?

choices.text: d_xy, d_xz and d_yz are higher (sigma antibonding) and d_z^2 and d_x^2−y^2 are nonbonding: the inverse of octahedral, with a somewhat smaller splitting
d_z^2 and d_x^2−y^2 are higher and d_xy, d_xz and d_yz lower, as in an octahedron
choices.why: The tetrahedral pattern is the inverse of the octahedral one. In a tetrahedron, d_xy, d_xz and d_yz lie closer to the ligands.

choices.text: d_xy, d_xz and d_yz are higher, with a larger splitting than in an octahedron, because they point directly at the ligands
choices.why: No d orbital points directly at the ligands in a tetrahedron, so overlap is weaker and the splitting is expected to be a little smaller.

choices.text: All five d orbitals stay degenerate, because they all lie off-axis
choices.why: Being off-axis doesn't make them equivalent: the edge-pointing orbitals are closer to the ligands (r) than the face-pointing ones (√2 r).

explanation: d_xy, d_xz and d_yz point at the cube's edges, a distance r from the ligands; d_z^2 and d_x^2−y^2 point at the faces, √2 r away. Group theory confirms that Γσ = A1 + T2, so the T2 set (d_xy, d_xz, d_yz) forms antibonding combinations and the E set (d_z^2, d_x^2−y^2) is nonbonding. Since no orbital points straight at the ligands, the splitting should be a little smaller than octahedral.

prompt: For sigma bonding in a tetrahedral complex (T_d, h = 24, classes E, 8C3, 3C2, 6S4, 6σd), the reducible representation is Γσ = 4, 1, 0, 0, 2. The T2 representation has characters 3, 0, −1, −1, 1. Using a_i = (1/h) Σ N∙χ(R)∙χ_i(R), how many times does T2 appear in Γσ?
explanation: a(T2) = (1/24)[1∙4∙3 + 8∙1∙0 + 3∙0∙(−1) + 6∙0∙(−1) + 6∙2∙1] = (1/24)(12 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 12) = 24/24 = 1. Together with one A1, this gives Γσ = A1 + T2, so d_xy, d_xz and d_yz (T2) are the d orbitals involved in sigma bonding.

prompt: Removing the two axial ligands from an octahedral complex gives a square planar complex. What happens to the d_z^2 orbital?

choices.text: It drops well below d_x^2−y^2 but not all the way to nonbonding, because its toroid still overlaps weakly with the ligands in the xy plane
It becomes the highest-energy d orbital
choices.why: The highest is d_x^2−y^2, which points straight at the four remaining ligands. d_z^2 loses its strong antibonding interaction along z.

choices.text: It drops all the way to the nonbonding level
choices.why: The d_z^2 toroid lies in the plane of the ligands, so some antibonding interaction remains.

choices.text: It stays degenerate with d_x^2−y^2
choices.why: The two were degenerate in the octahedron, but without the z-axis ligands d_z^2 drops well below d_x^2−y^2.

explanation: With no ligands on the z axis, d_z^2 no longer forms a strong antibonding combination along z, so it drops. Its toroid still lies in the plane of the x- and y-axis ligands, so it overlaps with them a little and doesn't reach the nonbonding level. d_x^2−y^2 remains the highest orbital, well above the rest.

prompt: In a square planar complex, the gap between d_x^2−y^2 and the next orbital down is much larger than the other splittings, so the four lower d orbitals fill before d_x^2−y^2. How many unpaired electrons does a square planar d^8 complex have?
explanation: Eight electrons fill the four lower orbitals with two electrons each, leaving d_x^2−y^2 empty. Every electron is paired: 0 unpaired electrons. This avoids populating the highest-energy orbital, which is why square planar complexes are so often d^8.

prompt: In a square planar complex (D4h), ligand p orbitals perpendicular to the plane give Γπ⊥ = A2u + B2u + Eg. Which metal d orbitals can pi bond with them?

choices.text: d_xz and d_yz
d_xy
choices.why: d_xy (B2g) pairs with the in-plane pi orbitals, Γπ|| = A2g + B2g + Eu.

choices.text: d_z^2 and d_x^2−y^2
choices.why: These match A1g and B1g, which appear in the sigma representation, Γσ = A1g + B1g + Eu.

choices.text: d_xy, d_xz and d_yz equally, as in an octahedron
choices.why: In D4h the in-plane and perpendicular pi orbitals aren't equivalent: d_xy pairs with in-plane pi orbitals, and d_xz and d_yz with perpendicular ones.

explanation: In the D4h character table, (xz, yz) transform as Eg and z as A2u, so the perpendicular pi orbitals match d_xz, d_yz and p_z. Overlap with d_xz and d_yz is much stronger than with p_z, so the d orbitals dominate.

prompt: Compared with chloride, how does a strongly pi-accepting ligand such as cyanide change the d orbital splittings in a homoleptic square planar palladium complex?

choices.text: The splittings get larger, by about 50%, because the d orbitals that pi bond to the acceptor drop in energy
The splittings get smaller, because the pi-bonding d orbitals are pushed up
choices.why: That's what pi donors like chloride do. Pi acceptors lower the pi-bonding d orbitals and widen the gaps.

choices.text: The splittings don't change, because square planar complexes have no pi bonding
choices.why: Square planar complexes can pi bond: d_xy, d_xz and d_yz have the right symmetry to interact with ligand pi orbitals.

choices.text: The splittings get larger, because the d_x^2−y^2 orbital drops to the bottom
choices.why: d_x^2−y^2 remains the highest orbital. It's the pi-bonding d orbitals that drop.

explanation: With a pi acceptor, the ligand π* orbital lies above the metal d orbital, so the metal d orbital becomes the lower, bonding combination and drops in energy. The gap between the pi-bonding metal orbitals and the purely sigma-antibonding ones widens. For the palladium complexes, the splittings are about 50% greater with cyanide than with chloride.
